message.content:
Below is a concise but comprehensive overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (All information is current as of 2026‑06‑28; laws can change, so it’s always a good idea to double‑check with a local attorney or the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs.) | # | Right / Protection | What it Means | Practical Tips | |---|--------------------|---------------|----------------| | **1** | **Security Deposit Limits** | Landlords may charge a maximum of **one month’s rent** for a single‑unit lease and **two months’ rent** for a multi‑unit lease. | Keep a copy of the lease and any receipt for the deposit. If you’re moving out, request a written itemized list of deductions. | | **2** | **Deposit Return** | Landlord must return the deposit (minus lawful deductions) within **30 days** after you move out, unless the lease specifies a longer period. | Ask for the return in writing. If the landlord fails to comply, you can file a claim in small‑claims court. | | **3** | **Habitability / Repairs** | Landlords must keep the premises in a safe, sanitary condition—plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, pest control, etc. | Document any repair requests in writing. If the landlord fails to act, you may withhold rent (in some cases) or pursue a “repair‑and‑deduct” remedy. | | **4** | **Notice Requirements for Entry** | Landlord must give **at least 24 hours’ written notice** before entering, except in emergencies. | Keep a log of all entries. If the landlord enters without notice, you can file a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office. | | **5** | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | If the landlord or neighbors disturb you, document incidents and consider mediation or legal action if necessary. | | **6** | **Anti‑Discrimination** | Under federal Fair Housing Act and Texas law, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | Keep records of any discriminatory remarks or actions. File a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **7** | **Lease Termination & Eviction** | • **Month‑to‑month**: Either party may terminate with **30 days’ written notice**.
• **Fixed‑term**: Landlord must provide notice at least **30 days** before the lease ends.
• **Eviction**: Landlord must follow the Texas Property Code §92.001‑92.006, which requires a written notice (e.g., 30‑day notice for nonpayment). | Keep copies of all notices. If you receive an eviction notice, you have the right to contest it in court. | | **8** | **Rent Increase Notice** | For month‑to‑month leases, landlords must give **30 days’ written notice** before raising rent. | Verify the notice is in writing and keep a copy. | | **9** | **Right to Repair & Deduct** | If the landlord fails to fix a major problem, you may pay for repairs and deduct the cost from your rent (subject to limits). | Obtain receipts and keep a detailed record of the issue and your payment. | | **10** | **Right to Disclose Health Hazards** | Landlords must disclose known health hazards (e.g., lead paint, mold). | Request a written disclosure form. If the landlord fails to disclose, you may have a claim for damages. | | **11** | **Right to Privacy** | Landlord cannot enter without notice, except in emergencies. | If the landlord enters without notice, you can file a complaint. | | **12** | **Right to a Written Lease** | While not required, having a written lease protects both parties. | Always sign a lease and keep a copy. | | **13** | **Right to File a Complaint** | You can file complaints with the Texas Attorney General’s Office, HUD, or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | Gather evidence (photos, emails, receipts) before filing. | | **14** | **Right to Mediation** | Many disputes can be resolved through mediation before going to court. | Contact the Texas Mediation Center or local community mediation services. | ### Quick Reference Checklist 1. **Read the lease** – note rent amount, deposit, notice periods, and any special clauses. 2. **Document everything** – photos of conditions, written repair requests, receipts, and correspondence. 3. **Know the timelines** – 30‑day notice for entry, rent increases, lease termination, and deposit return. 4. **Keep copies** – of all documents, notices, and communications. 5. **Know your recourse** – small‑claims court, mediation, or filing a formal complaint. ### Useful Resources | Resource | What It Offers | How to Access | |----------|----------------|---------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | Handles complaints about landlord‑tenant disputes. | https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection | | **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** | Fair Housing complaints. | https://www.hud.gov/ | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | Discrimination complaints. | https://www.tchra.org/ | | **Texas Small Claims Court** | Resolve disputes up to $20,000. | https://www.txcourts.gov/small-claims/ | | **Local Mediation Centers** | Free or low‑cost mediation services. | Search online for “mediation center” + your city. | | **Texas Property Code** | Full statutory text. | https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/ | --- #### Bottom Line As a Texas tenant, you have strong statutory protections regarding deposits, habitability, privacy, anti‑discrimination, and fair notice. By keeping thorough records, understanding the required notice periods, and knowing where to file complaints or seek mediation, you can effectively enforce your rights and resolve most disputes without needing to go to court. If you encounter a complex situation or feel your rights are being violated, consider consulting a local attorney who specializes in landlord‑tenant law.
